verses.text: Yahweh says: “For three transgressions of Moab, yes, for four, I will not turn away its punishment; because he burned the bones of the king of Edom into lime;
but I will send a fire on Moab, and it will devour the palaces of Kerioth; and Moab will die with tumult, with shouting, and with the sound of the trumpet;
and I will cut off the judge from among them, and will kill all its princes with him,”  says Yahweh.

Yahweh says: “For three transgressions of Judah, yes, for four, I will not turn away its punishment; because they have rejected Yahweh’s law, and have not kept his statutes, and their lies have led them astray, after which their fathers walked;
But I will send a fire on Judah, and it will devour the palaces of Jerusalem.”
Yahweh says: “For three transgressions of Israel, yes, for four, I will not turn away its punishment; because they have sold the righteous for silver, and the needy for a pair of shoes;
They trample on the dust of the earth on the head of the poor, and deny justice to the oppressed; and a man and his father use the same maiden, to profane my holy name;
and they lay themselves down beside every altar on clothes taken in pledge; and in the house of their God  they drink the wine of those who have been fined.
Yet I destroyed the Amorite before them, whose height was like the height of the cedars, and he was strong as the oaks; yet I destroyed his fruit from above, and his roots from beneath.
Also I brought you up out of the land of Egypt, and led you forty years in the wilderness, to possess the land of the Amorite.
I raised up some of your sons for prophets, and some of your young men for Nazirites. Isn’t this true, you children of Israel?” says Yahweh.
“But you gave the Nazirites wine to drink, and commanded the prophets, saying, ‘Don’t prophesy!’
Behold,  I will crush you in your place, as a cart crushes that is full of grain.
Flight will perish from the swift; and the strong won’t strengthen his force; neither shall the mighty deliver himself;
neither shall he stand who handles the bow; and he who is swift of foot won’t escape; neither shall he who rides the horse deliver himself;
and he who is courageous among the mighty will flee away naked on that day,”  says Yahweh.

footnotes.content: God speaks judgment on Moab first, a nation east of the Jordan. The pattern is set: 'for three transgressions, yes, for four'—a way of saying there's more than enough wrong to demand account. Even the desecration of the dead, burning the king's bones, does not escape His notice. Mercy has its limits where injustice ripens fully.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Kerioth, the capital fortress—a real place where Moab's power sat. Fire will devour it, and the tumult will be loud. There is no hiding from the sound of judgment. All the noise and terror that sin breeds will finally echo back.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The judge and princes—Moab's wisdom and strength—will be cut off together. There's something merciful even in this: they who led the people astray cannot go on leading. Justice cuts at the root of corruption.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now God turns to Judah—His own people. They rejected His law, neglected His statutes. Worse, they believed lies about what was true and good, the very lies their ancestors had embraced. We can know the Lord's Word and still turn away from it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jerusalem, the holy city itself—her palaces will burn. The place where God's name was invoked will not be spared because His people abandoned His way. Proximity to truth is no shield against its judgment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Israel's sin laid bare: they sell the innocent for silver, the hungry for a pair of shoes. So little purchased so great a betrayal. When profit becomes our god, the poorest pay the price.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They trample the dust, which is the poor person's lot—then deny them justice. And a man and his father share a maiden to profane God's holy name. The accumulation shows a people unraveling: each sin deepens the next, until sacred things are treated as common.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They recline beside altars on clothes seized as collateral from the poor—using their neighbor's last possession as a cushion while worshiping. They drink wine purchased by fines levied on others. Worship without justice is a lie we tell ourselves in God's house.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God reminds them: He destroyed the Amorite, great as cedars, strong as oaks. He cleared the land for them—root and branch. This is the God who brought you in. Will you now forget the Hand that upheld you?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Forty years in the wilderness—a real journey, not a metaphor. God led them through hard country to give them the land. Every meal, every plague averted, every morning light was His provision. We do well to remember what we have been saved from and given.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Prophets and Nazirites—God raised them up, men set apart to speak truth and live holy lives. These were His gifts to call the people back. Yet Israel will silence them. We sometimes want the comfort of knowing God without the challenge of His Word.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Israel seduced the Nazirites with wine and commanded the prophets to be silent. Offering temptation to those devoted to holiness, and censoring those sent to warn—this is not mere sin but a turning against God's own witnesses.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God says He will crush them as a loaded cart crushes grain beneath its weight. The image is stark: they cannot stand under the weight of His judgment. When mercy is rejected, the ground itself cannot hold us up.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Flight will perish from the swift. The strong will have no strength. Amos paints a helpless scene—the very qualities men rely on will fail them. In the day of reckoning, human prowess is hollow.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The archer cannot stand, the swift cannot escape, the horseman cannot save himself. Each skill becomes useless. This is what it means to face judgment without repentance—all our defenses crumble.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even the bravest will flee naked in that day. Looking back from a longer road, readers today hear an echo: we cannot hide from God, and the trappings of power mean nothing before Him. In our own time, this still speaks—how often do we cling to status or strength as if they could shield us from truth?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
